strengths: The paper presents a clear and practically motivated Algorithms/General contribution: CASA modifies cross-attention fusion by allowing local text-to-text attention within multimodal fusion windows, aiming to retain cross-attention scalability while recovering much of token insertion performance.

The empirical evaluation is broad and unusually relevant to the claim. The authors evaluate training from a text-only LLM, adapting a pretrained Qwen2.5-VL model, image benchmarks, video benchmarks, ablations against vanilla/gated cross-attention, token-compression baselines, and streaming-captioning efficiency.

The main controlled ablations are convincing in showing that standard cross-attention underperforms badly on high-resolution document/chart/OCR tasks, while CASA substantially improves this regime under similar training setups.
The efficiency motivation is strong. The paper explains why avoiding image tokens in the LLM KV cache and FFNs matters, and supports this with memory/time measurements and streaming inference plots.
The method is simple, modular, and likely useful to practitioners who need long-context or streaming multimodal inference and cannot afford full visual-token insertion.
weaknesses: The central claim that CASA largely closes the gap to token insertion is only partially supported. CASA remains notably behind token insertion on several fine-grained tasks, especially InfoVQA and ChartQA, and the adapted Qwen2.5-VL CASA model drops substantially on InfoVQA, AI2D, and MME.

Some comparisons are confounded by different training budgets, data, resolutions, and sequence lengths. For example, CASA-He uses 0.3T training tokens while the insertion Helium baseline uses 0.1T, and insertion baselines are sometimes constrained to lower resolution or shorter sequences because of memory limits. This is practically relevant, but it complicates pure architectural attribution.

The mechanism explanation is suggestive rather than fully established. The self-masking inference ablation shows the trained model relies on self-attention, but it does not by itself prove the proposed implicit gating explanation; attention visualizations averaged over heads/layers are also a weak diagnostic.

The live video captioning evaluation is promising but not fully rigorous: it relies on GPT-4o judging against reported baselines, lacks stronger human or task-specific metrics, and the qualitative examples include factual/hallucination issues, suggesting caption quality remains fragile despite efficiency gains.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript as provided: the project page placeholders appear blank, and the large-scale training setup requires substantial compute. More precise release details, scripts, model checkpoints, and evaluation commands would be important.

The paper would benefit from a more explicit limitations discussion, especially about residual failures on high-resolution reasoning, dependence on a strong Qwen2.5-VL vision encoder, data overlap risks across large public VLM mixtures, and societal risks of real-time video captioning.

strengths: The paper addresses an important efficiency problem in VLM fusion: avoiding the high KV-cache and FFN costs of token insertion while preserving fine-grained visual understanding.

CASA is simple and easy to understand: the method augments cross-attention by allowing local causal text-to-text attention in the visual injection layer, making it potentially modular for both new VLM training and adaptation of existing insertion-based VLMs.

The manuscript includes several useful ablations, including comparisons against vanilla/gated cross-attention, CASA placement variants, token compression baselines, and an inference-time masking study suggesting that the self-attention component is important.
The paper evaluates on a reasonably broad set of image and video benchmarks and reports practical memory/latency measurements for streaming video settings, which is relevant to the claimed use case.
weaknesses: The central idea is quite incremental: CASA is essentially cross-attention over concatenated visual tokens and a local text window, resembling an added local self-attention/cross-attention block. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish this from obvious decoder-attention variants or prior multimodal attention designs beyond empirical comparisons.

Several comparisons are not fully convincing. CASA models often use different training budgets, resolutions, sequence lengths, or data mixtures than insertion baselines and external cross-attention models. For example, Table 2 reports CASA trained with more tokens than the insertion Helium baseline, while insertion is constrained to lower resolution/shorter sequences. This weakens claims about closing the gap under controlled conditions.

The efficiency claims are overstated for some settings. CASA clearly reduces KV-cache growth and avoids FFNs on image tokens, but the reported training time for CASA+ is nearly the same as insertion in Table 1, and the practical advantage depends on giving insertion a constrained setup. Theoretical cost notation is also confusing/inconsistent in places, making it hard to audit the scaling argument.

The adapted Qwen2.5-VL results still show substantial degradation on important fine-grained benchmarks, especially InfoVQA, AI2D, and MME. Describing this as recovering most performance understates the cost of replacing insertion with CASA for applications where these capabilities matter.

The streaming video captioning evidence is relatively weak. The quantitative evaluation relies on GPT-4o-as-judge and comparisons to reported baselines rather than a thoroughly controlled setup, and the qualitative examples include apparent hallucinations and temporal incoherence. This does not strongly establish real-world captioning quality, only better memory behavior.

The paper would benefit from stronger baselines against modern efficient insertion approaches, KV-cache compression/pruning, context-extension methods, and compressed-token VLMs under matched latency/memory budgets. The Q-Former compression baseline is useful but not sufficient to rule out competitive alternatives.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the submitted manuscript: the project page placeholders appear blank in the PDF, and the release is promised rather than available for review. Given the heavy dependence on large-scale training details and curated data mixtures, this is a meaningful concern.

The manuscript does not adequately discuss possible benchmark/data contamination from large curated mixtures such as FineVision and LLaVA-OneVision subsets, despite evaluating on chart, document, OCR, and VQA benchmarks that may overlap with common training sources.

strengths: The paper identifies a clear and practically important weakness of cross-attention VLM fusion: standard cross-attention is efficient but underperforms token insertion on fine-grained document, chart, and OCR-heavy tasks. The proposed CASA mechanism is simple, well motivated, and directly targets this gap by allowing local text-to-text attention inside the visual fusion layer.

The empirical evidence is broad and generally convincing. The authors evaluate training from a text-only LLM, adapting a strong pretrained token-insertion VLM, image and video benchmarks, and a streaming video captioning setting. CASA consistently improves over standard and gated cross-attention, especially on high-resolution/detail-sensitive benchmarks.

The ablations are useful and support the central claim. Comparisons against vanilla cross-attention, gated cross-attention, CASA variants, Q-Former compression, image-embedding FFN updates, and inference-time masking of self-attention all point to the importance of the text self-attention component.

The work has real systems significance. CASA preserves much of the efficiency appeal of cross-attention, avoids growing the LLM KV cache with image tokens, and is particularly compelling for streaming or long multimodal contexts where token insertion becomes costly.

The paper is clearly written, with good motivation, intuitive diagrams, and enough implementation detail to understand the attention pattern, sequence packing, training setup, and practical memory/speed tradeoffs.
weaknesses: CASA does not fully close the gap to token insertion. The remaining drops are substantial on some fine-grained tasks, e.g. InfoVQA and AI2D when adapting Qwen2.5-VL, and ChartQA/InfoVQA for the Helium-based models. The paper is honest about this, but the title-level framing of closing the gap is somewhat stronger than the results justify.

Some comparisons are not perfectly controlled. Token-insertion baselines are sometimes trained at lower resolution or shorter sequence length due to memory limits, while CASA uses more image tokens or more training tokens in some settings. This reflects real constraints, but makes it harder to isolate architectural quality from training-budget and resolution effects.

The method is conceptually simple and close to existing cross-attention/self-attention machinery. Its originality lies more in the diagnosis, design combination, and empirical validation than in a fundamentally new modeling primitive.

The live video captioning evaluation is promising but not as rigorous as the image benchmark evaluation. It relies heavily on LLM-as-judge scores and qualitative examples, with limited analysis of caption factuality, temporal consistency, or failure modes. The comparison to insertion-based streaming models also uses compressed Q-Former baselines rather than strongest possible long-video systems.

The reproducibility story is partly deferred to a project page, and the manuscript text shows blank project-page placeholders. The training setup also requires substantial compute, so smaller-scale reproduction or public scripts/checkpoints would be important for practical verification.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely efficiency problem in VLMs: token-insertion fusion has serious memory and latency costs for multi-image and streaming-video settings, while cross-attention is underexplored in modern pipelines.

The decomposition of cross-attention versus token insertion into five design differences is clear and useful. It helps separate architectural effects from implementation/training-pipeline effects, and gives the paper more value than a pure benchmark comparison.

The empirical study is fairly broad: the authors train CA models from a text-only LLM, adapt a strong insertion-based Qwen2.5-VL model, evaluate image and video benchmarks, and include efficiency measurements, ablations, and a live-captioning application.

The central empirical finding is meaningful: simple CA variants trained in comparable modern settings come close to token insertion on many benchmarks while giving large inference-time memory/latency advantages, especially for streaming video.
The paper is generally well written and reproducibility is helped by detailed training/data descriptions, benchmark lists, and an stated intent to release inference code and trained models.
weaknesses: The algorithmic novelty is moderate. Much of the contribution is a careful re-evaluation and adaptation of known cross-attention mechanisms rather than a fundamentally new architecture or theory.

The strongest CA results still show notable gaps on important fine-grained tasks, especially InfographicVQA, ChartQA, and parts of document/chart understanding. These are central computer-vision VLM capabilities, so the limitations should temper the broad claim that vanilla CA is nearly competitive.

Some fairness aspects of the controlled comparison remain imperfect. For token insertion, memory constraints lead to shorter per-device sequence lengths, and for Qwen2.5-VL adaptation the comparison is between a frozen base model and added CA layers rather than a fully matched adaptation budget across fusion types.

The streaming-video evidence is promising but somewhat narrow. Live-captioning evaluation relies on a GPT-4o judge on LiveSports3K, and comparisons to specialized streaming/pruning/KV-compression methods are limited; stronger baselines would better support the real-world deployment claims.

The proposed use of delimiter tokens as implicit gist tokens is interesting but under-analyzed. The paper would benefit from ablations on the number/type of gist tokens, windowing choices, and failure cases where compressed visual history is insufficient.

Several presentation issues reduce polish: there are typographical errors, some extracted symbols/notation are awkward, the abstract's project-page link appears missing, and some qualitative live-captioning examples contain clear hallucinations or contradictions. These do not invalidate the work but should be cleaned up.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important question: whether cross-attention can be a competitive and more efficient alternative to token insertion for VLM fusion, especially in long-context and streaming video settings.

The comparison is more controlled than much prior discussion: the authors train both insertion and cross-attention variants under similar pipelines from a text-only Helium1-2B backbone, and also adapt Qwen2.5-VL-3B, which makes the empirical case more informative than simply comparing unrelated published models.

The decomposition into design differences D1-D5 is useful and clarifies where efficiency gains come from, including parameter sharing, local text/image attention, replacing self-attention layers, image-token updates, and visual history handling.

The experiments cover many standard image and video benchmarks, include ablations over CA variants, layer frequency, image-token updates, token compression, and resolution, and show consistent efficiency advantages in memory/latency for streaming scenarios.
The paper is generally clear and well organized, and the practical live video captioning demonstration makes the motivation concrete.
weaknesses: The originality is moderate. The core mechanism is not new, and the main contribution is largely an empirical revisit plus engineering adaptation. The D1-D5 taxonomy is helpful but not a deep theoretical contribution, and several components such as gist-like tokens, CA windows, and FFN visual updates are inherited or closely related to prior work.

The strongest claims rely on a limited set of backbones and training recipes. Results are shown mainly for Helium1-2B and Qwen2.5-VL-3B; it is unclear whether the conclusions hold for larger VLMs, different vision encoders, different data mixtures, or stronger modern token-compression baselines.

The comparison to prior cross-attention models is not fully clean because models differ in data, scale, training tokens, architecture, and evaluation settings. Although the authors reproduce some baselines, the paper sometimes uses these comparisons to support broad claims about state-of-the-art CA models without fully isolating confounders.

Important performance gaps remain on chart/document/infographic understanding, exactly where high-resolution visual detail matters. The paper acknowledges this, but the limitation weakens the general claim that simple CA is nearly competitive with insertion.

The streaming/live-captioning evidence is suggestive but not fully convincing. The quantitative quality evaluation uses LLM-as-judge on a narrow benchmark, lacks human validation or statistical uncertainty, and the reported CA model still trails the stronger LiveCC baselines despite being more efficient.

Reproducibility is only partially supported. The manuscript says code/models or a project page will be released, but the abstract contains an incomplete project-page reference, and many details needed to exactly reproduce data filtering, packing, and training at 64 H100 scale remain hard to verify.

There are presentation and polish issues, including malformed symbols in extracted text, typos, inconsistent table notation, and some unclear phrasing around training-token equality and batch/sequence trade-offs. These do not invalidate the work but reduce confidence in the final manuscript quality.

strengths: The paper presents a timely and useful re-evaluation of cross-attention for VLM fusion, challenging the common assumption that token insertion is inherently much stronger. The decomposition into five design differences between cross-attention and token insertion is clear and helps make the comparison scientifically interpretable rather than only empirical.

The experimental design is stronger than typical architecture-comparison papers: the authors train a token-insertion Helium baseline and several CA variants under largely matched conditions, and also study adaptation from a strong pretrained Qwen2.5-VL model. This makes the central claim, that simple CA is more competitive than previously reported, reasonably convincing.

The efficiency argument is well motivated and practically important. The memory/latency advantages are not just asymptotic; they are tied to measured training/inference costs and demonstrated in a streaming video captioning setting where token-insertion KV caches become problematic.

The paper includes broad evaluation across document/chart understanding, OCR, general VQA, video QA, and live captioning, plus useful ablations on parameter sharing, CA frequency, FFN updates, image resolution, and token compression. The discussion of where CA still struggles, especially InfographicVQA and chart-like tasks, is appropriately nuanced.

The work is likely to have impact because it offers a simple path for converting or training efficient VLMs without many bespoke architectural additions, and it may encourage more careful comparisons of fusion mechanisms in long-context and streaming multimodal applications.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic novelty is moderate. Much of the contribution is a controlled empirical study and practical adaptation recipe rather than a substantially new fusion mechanism; this is still valuable, but it makes the case depend heavily on the experimental protocol.

Some fairness details remain imperfect. Token insertion is trained with shorter per-device sequence lengths and different accumulation to fit memory, while CA uses a different attention/windowing structure; the authors argue token counts are matched, but residual differences in optimization dynamics, packing, and batch composition could affect the comparison.

The adapted Qwen2.5-VL CA model still has a substantial gap on fine-grained document/chart benchmarks, especially InfographicVQA, where the drop is large. This limitation is acknowledged, but it narrows the scope of the claim that CA is broadly competitive.

The streaming-captioning evaluation is promising but not fully satisfying. The quantitative captioning result relies on an LLM-as-judge benchmark, and the qualitative examples show factual errors and unstable captions, so the live-captioning evidence mainly supports efficiency rather than high caption quality.

The paper uses very large training resources and large curated public data mixtures, which may limit reproducibility for many groups. More details on released checkpoints, exact data filtering, evaluation prompts, and implementation would be important for reproducing the controlled comparisons.

The analysis of visual history via gist/post-image delimiter tokens is intriguing but under-isolated. It would be useful to ablate the number/type of gist tokens and test harder multi-image reasoning cases to better understand when the local-window CA assumption breaks down.
